title: Fragmented Token Handshake and Rollback Protocol
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc explores a concrete protocol for emitting fragmented (partial) token payloads in the serving runtime while preserving safety for KV cache, scheduling preemption, and cancellation/rollback. It is intended as a mid-stage engineering draft to align runtime, transport, and SRE on semantics for: chunking semantics, flush policies, cancellable partials, and KV commit/rollback interactions.

Motivation:
- We often need to surface output progressively to clients (reduced perceived latency) while performing downstream commits (KV cache, attention state) that must be consistent if a request is later cancelled or replaced.
- Existing streaming designs assume either: (a) every emitted token is final and durable, or (b) nothing is durable until the stream ends. Both extremes are costly (latency or recomputation).
- This draft proposes a middle path: a handshake-based fragment/commit protocol with lightweight snapshots that lets us stream partial tokens while supporting fast cancellation and safe KV cache state.

Goals and constraints:
- Low-latency first byte(s) to client while preserving ability to rollback recent speculative state without global stalls.
- Minimal extra RT (round-trip) overhead for common-case (no cancellation).
- Clear, observable semantics for tracing and billing: what emitted tokens are billable/committed vs speculative.
- Compatible with existing kernel scheduling: batching, preemption, and small-kernel fast paths.
- Conservative memory footprint for ephemeral snapshots.

Key concepts / vocabulary:
- fragment: a contiguous sequence of output bytes/tokens emitted as a unit. Fragments are addressed by (seq, frag_id).
- soft-commit: local runtime decision that makes a fragment more durable for routing/fallback but still reversible with a lightweight rollback.
- hard-commit: final durability: fragment is persistent for billing, analytics, and KV state is considered committed. Equivalent to end-of-response or explicit commit marker.
- ephemeral-kv-snapshot: a copy-on-write lightweight view of KV cache state associated with a serving request; used to roll back speculative updates.
- rollback-watermark: sequence id up to which state must be reverted when cancellation occurs.
- continuation-handle: small token returned to client for resumable streams (used in pause/resume flows).

Protocol overview (happy path):
1) Request arrives and enters scheduler. Kernel selection and batching are determined.
2) Runtime prepares an ephemeral-kv-snapshot S0 for the request; S0 is initially just a view pointer (no deep copy).
3) Runtime begins generation and emits fragment F0 (first partial tokens) with header: {seq:0, frag:0, tentative:true, kv_snapshot_id:S0.id}. This is streamed immediately to client.
4) If generation continues and fragment boundaries are crossed, runtime produces F1, F2... Emitted fragments are tagged tentative=true until either a soft-commit or hard-commit is performed.
5) When the model reaches a safe commit point (see heuristics below), runtime performs a soft-commit for fragments up to frag=k. Soft-commit does two things: (a) marks fragments as durable for routing/fallback; (b) materializes small copy-on-write edits in the ephemeral-kv-snapshot so reads/writes see the committed view while still supporting rollback.
6) If the request completes normally, a hard-commit marker is emitted and KV snapshot is merged into the global KV cache (durable). Billing is attributed to hard-committed tokens.

Heuristics for commit points:
- Natural language boundaries: sentence end, punctuation, newline, or other token-level heuristics.
- Kernel boundary: after a full decoder loop where the KV cache update is idempotent and does not cross attention window limits.
- Resource pressure: if scheduler preemption is likely (high queue delay), prefer soft-commits to make partial progress durable for fallback.
- Age threshold: if a fragment has been tentative for N ms and downstream consumers expect progress, convert to soft-commit to avoid rework.

Cancellation and rollback semantics:
- Cancellation signal may arrive from client or SLO watchdog. Two paths: fast-cancel vs graceful-cancel.
  - fast-cancel: immediately stop generation; mark rollback-watermark = latest tentative fragment seq; discard ephemeral snapshot (cheap COW discard). Tell transport layer to send cancellation ack. Partial tokens that were only tentative are considered non-billable and flagged as incomplete.
  - graceful-cancel: request indicates finish-without-final-commit. Runtime may choose to soft-commit trailing fragments before stopping (e.g., if already past a commit heuristic).
- If the runtime has performed a soft-commit but not hard-commit, rollback must revert ephemeral-kv changes but preserve any global KV cache invariants. We use a two-stage undo log: small per-request delta + application of inverse ops on rollback.
- Hard-commit cannot be rolled back. Any cancellation after hard-commit only affects subsequent requests.

KV cache interaction patterns:
- Reads: always consult ephemeral snapshot first then fall back to global cache. This ensures speculative local writes do not leak across requests.
- Writes: write into ephemeral snapshot. On soft-commit we convert writes into a small durable manifest (not merged globally) and mark the fragment(s) as durable for routing with a reference to the manifest.
- Merge: on hard-commit, apply manifest to global KV cache using idempotent merge routines. If merge collides with different concurrent writes, runtime guarantees last-writer semantics keyed by request timestamp and seq.
- Eviction safety: manifests are kept until either hard-commit completes or time-to-live expires. Eviction must account for manifests referenced by continuation-handles.

Scheduling and kernel concerns:
- Kernel preemption: long-running kernels must periodically checkpoint minimal generator state so fragments can be emitted even across kernel switches. Checkpoints align with fragment boundaries to avoid partial-kernel emissions.
- Batching: when coalescing multiple requests into a batch, fragment headers include batch-id and local-index so reassembly and rollback can be applied per-request. Speculative emissions from batched runs are segregated by ephemeral snapshot.
- Small-kernel fast path: optimize the common short-response case by avoiding full snapshot materialization until after first fragment emission. Use lazy COW-on-write to keep latency low.

Transport and client expectations:
- Fragment header fields (transport-level): seq, frag_id, tentative|soft|hard, kv_manifest_id (optional), continuation_handle (optional), tentative_ttl (ms).
- Clients must be informed that tentative fragments may be retracted (e.g., replaced by corrected tokens) and should be prepared to accept patch messages.
- For resumable streams, continuation_handle allows client to reattach and request resumption from last hard-commit or specific frag seq.

Partial-token atomicity and fragmentation rules:
- We avoid splitting UTF-8 codepoints across fragments. Fragment boundaries should align to token boundaries where possible. If byte-level streaming is required, we include byte-offset metadata and a finalizing fragment that completes a split codepoint.
- Partial tokens emitted (in the middle of a token) are marked 'subtoken' and are always tentative and non-billable until the token finalizes in a subsequent fragment. This avoids charging for incorrectly generated tokens.

Observability (what to surface):
- fragment_emit events: seq, frag_id, tentative/soft/hard, kv_manifest_id, kernel_id, batch_id, timestamp.
- rollback events: request_id, rollback_watermark, reason (client_cancel|slo|error), kv_reverts_count.
- metrics: tentative_token_count, soft_commits_per_min, hard_commits_per_min, avg_rollback_latency.
- Tracing: attach frag lifecycle span to the request trace (emit -> soft-commit -> hard-commit/rollback).

Billing semantics (proposal):
- Bill only for hard-committed tokens.
- Optionally provide a preview billing metric for tentative tokens for customer visibility but not invoiced.
- In special enterprise mode (low latency, higher cost), allow billing at soft-commit time if customer explicitly opts in; document the risk of later rollback and cost adjustments.

Prototype notes and microbench plan:
- Implement COW ephemeral-kv-snapshot using versioned hash map (shared ptr + diffs).
- Benchmark scenarios: no-cancel short (<=32 tokens), no-cancel long (>=512 tokens), cancellation at 20%, 50%, 90% progress, high concurrency (1000 qps) with small kernels and batching enabled.
- Measure: extra memory per request, rollback latency, percent of fragments soft-committed, throughput drop under mix.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How big can ephemeral manifests be without causing unacceptable memory pressure? We need empirical caps and eviction policies.
- Can we tighten billing semantics so customers have predictable spend when tentative tokens are common?
- Should soft-commits be automatically converted to hard-commits by a background merger for long-lived manifests? That could reduce read complexity but increases merge churn.
- How do we integrate with Dedicated / Private deployments where KV cache is external and has its own durability semantics?

Appendix: example fragment exchange (JSON wire sketch)
- Emitted fragment (tentative):
  {
    "req_id":"r-1", "seq":0, "frag_id":0, "tentative":true, "kv_snapshot":"s-1", "payload":"The quick br"
  }
- Next fragment completes a token and soft-commits:
  {
    "req_id":"r-1", "seq":1, "frag_id":1, "soft_commit":true, "kv_manifest":"m-57", "payload":"own fox jumps"
  }
- Cancellation and rollback ack:
  {
    "req_id":"r-1", "action":"cancel_ack", "rollback_watermark":1, "reason":"client_cancel"
  }

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative on semantics to avoid surprising data leaks or billing disputes. Feedback welcome especially around the soft-commit heuristics and manifest lifetime.
- Please comment in the GitHub PR (linked above) or drop design questions in #serving-runtime-streaming on Slack.

End of draft.
